result:
There's a box in my childhood closet that I think about more often than I should.

It wasn't a special box. It was a shoebox, Adidas, size 9, with the corners going soft from humidity and handling. Inside it were things that a ten-year-old considers to be treasure: a smooth black river stone with a white stripe all the way around it, like an equator; three deeply scratched-up marbles that I was convinced were lucky; a plastic sheriff's badge from a birthday party; a folded, yellowing note that said "Meet at the tree after school - J" in handwriting I could no longer place; a ticket stub from a movie I didn't remember seeing.

I haven't seen that box in twenty-five years. My parents moved. The closet was cleaned out. It's gone, in the landfill-and-dust sense of gone. And yet it has more permanence in my mind than almost any object I currently own. I can still see the way the lid didn't quite fit anymore, how it bowed up in the middle.

We think we own things. We think we live in places and have jobs and relationships and histories. But for the most part, we are just temporary custodians of things that are passing through.

Consider your apartment or house. Someone lived there before you. Someone will live there after you. You will paint a wall a color you love, a deep green or a warm terracotta, and you will feel an absurd amount of pride about it, and then one day you will paint it white again so the next person can imagine their own life there. You will fix a leaky faucet and never get thanked. You will leave a tiny scratch on the hardwood floor from dragging in a couch, and years from now someone else will wonder how it got there and invent a story for it.

This custodianship applies to everything, but nothing makes it clearer than objects. There is a Japanese concept called *tsukumogami* - the idea that everyday objects, after 100 years, gain a soul. A lantern, a teacup, a pair of sandals. I love that idea not because I believe my toaster is going to wake up and start talking, but because it correctly identifies that objects have lives that are longer and stranger than ours. That ceramic mug you drink coffee from was clay in a hillside for a million years. It was shaped by hands you will never meet, glazed in a factory, shipped across an ocean in a container with ten thousand identical mugs, purchased by someone who gave it to you for your birthday. You will drink from it every morning for eight years until you chip it and, feeling a brief and irrational guilt, throw it away. And then it will sit in a landfill for another thousand years. Your eight years with it were a blip. A short-term rental.

Once you start seeing the world this way, you can't stop.

Look at books. Every used book is a record of custodians. An old paperback I found last year had three different names written in the front, each crossed out. There was a coffee stain on page 42 that had warped the text into a little hill. Someone had underlined in angry red pen the line "we all make our own prisons." Another person, in much softer pencil, had written in the margin next to it: "but we have the key??" I have never felt more connected to two total strangers. I added my own custodial mark - a bus ticket I used as a bookmark and forgot to remove - and then I left it on a bench for someone else to find. I hope they kept the ticket.

We are custodians of stories, too. My grandmother used to tell a story about how she, as a little girl during the war, traded a single egg for a whole bar of chocolate and thought she had committed the greatest heist in human history. She told that story at every holiday, every birthday, until we could all recite it word for word. When she died, I thought the story would die with her, but at her funeral my cousin stood up and told it, and he got one detail wrong - he said it was two eggs - and three aunts corrected him at once. The story didn't belong to her. It never did. It belonged to the family, and now it's ours to carry, and to get slightly wrong, until we hand it off again.

Language itself works like this. Every word you have ever used was invented by someone else. You didn't come up with "nostalgia" or "petrichor" or "awkward." You inherited them. You borrowed them. You string them together in a sentence that feels uniquely yours, but the words themselves are ancient hand-me-downs. Even slang, which feels so new and ours, is just us temporarily holding sounds in our mouths before they go out of fashion and become embarrassing for the next generation.

Even our bodies are custodial. The water in your body right now has been rain, has been river, has been ocean, has been dinosaur blood, has been glacier. The calcium in your bones was once stone. The air you just inhaled was just exhaled by the person on the train next to you, and before that by a tree, and before that by a volcano. You are not a sealed container. You are a thoroughfare. You are a place where the universe is briefly taking the shape of a person so it can look around for a while.

This sounds melancholy, but I don't think it is. In fact, I think it's the opposite. If you really are just a custodian - of your house, your objects, your stories, your body, your little patch of time - then the job isn't to hold on tightly. The job isn't to own. The job is to take care of things while you have them, and to leave them a little better than you found them.

You wash the borrowed mug. You repair the chair before you pass it on. You listen carefully to the story so you can tell it right later, or at least tell it with love when you get it wrong. You plant a tree whose shade you will never sit in. You clean up a park you don't own.

There is a freedom in this. The pressure to achieve something permanent, something that will last forever with your name on it, falls away. Nothing lasts forever with your name on it. Even the pyramids are losing their corners to the wind. Even Shakespeare will one day be unreadable. But small acts of custodianship ripple forward in ways we can't trace.

That black river stone with the white equator around it - I wonder where it is now. Probably buried under layers of other trash, under coffee grounds and broken plastic. But for a few years, a child thought it was a planet. He kept it safe in a shoebox. He showed it to his friends and said, "Look, it's Saturn." And for those few years, because he believed it, it was.

We all get a little box of time. Inside it we put our lucky marbles and our ticket stubs and our smooth stones. We carry it for a while, thinking its contents are ours. And then, gently or not, we hand the box off - empty or full - to whoever is standing next to us, and we go on our way.
